newsitem.title: USA: American Air meets with pilots on contract talks.
newsitem.headline: American Air meets with pilots on contract talks.

text.p: Senior executives at American Airlines met with pilots' union leaders on Thursday to discuss their positions ahead of full-blown negotiations aimed at staving off a damaging strike.

The Allied Pilots Association, which says it will strike the airline from Feb. 15 unless a new labour contract deal is reached before then, said Thursday's meeting would not involve detailed negotiations.

"We are going to explain our position and listen to theirs before we go into next week's negotiations," a senior union official said. "The idea is that both sides know where we stand so we don't stumble into a strike because of any misunderstanding."
He said the pilots' union sees a 50 percent possibility of strike action, and that it could last up to 60 days.
The meeting began at 10 a.m. EST and was expected to last four or five hours.

Starting Monday, the two sides are to begin five days of "supermediation" in a last-gasp effort to reach a new four-year labour contract. Those negotiations will take place in Washington with the help of the National Mediation Board.

Pilots are demanding pay raises of more than 11 percent over the life of the contract, improved stock options and a guarantee that American will not use its American Eagle commuter carrier, which employs pilots of another union, to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

In a tentative agreement reached last September, the airline offered a 5 percent wage increase over four years and stock options but reserved the right to equip American Eagle with regional jets. Pilots' union leaders at first accepted that deal, but rank-and-file members rejected it in a surprise vote last month.
American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp. , says the pilots' new demands would cost the carrier an additional $200 million per year and would destroy its efforts to remain competitive.
The APA disputes that figure, saying its proposal would cost an additional $285 million over five years.

At Thursday's meeting, both sides were expected to explain how they arrived at their conflicting cost analyses. AMR Corp. President Don Carty and Chief Financial Officer Gerard Arpey were to attend the meeting, while APA President Jim Sovich was to lead the union's team.

Airline executives have repeatedly urged the pilots to accept binding arbitration, but union leaders have declined, saying they want to win a new contract now, even if it involves strike action, rather than risk lengthy arbitration.
AMR's stock gained $1.125 to $80 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
